items.title: Graphic Design in Japan: Mapping a Generation
items.note: Eighteen Japanese studios and designers born between 1970 and 1990, drawn from about twenty interviews Dimos has done since 2018. It skips the Yokoo and Tanaka history lesson and looks at how this generation works now, across culture and commerce with no hard line between them. Most of the work hasn't been seen much in Europe. 192 pages, from Éditions B42.

items.title: Women's Rights are Human Rights
items.note: International posters on gender inequality, violence and reproductive rights, by dozens of designers and agencies. Resnick introduces it and Steven Heller adds a text. 224 pages, 23 x 30 cm, from Set Margins'. This week's poster pick, and a reminder of what a poster can still do when it has something to say.

items.title: Letterform Frequencies: Exploring the Visual Imprint of Arabic Type
items.note: Nammour runs the Arabic Type Research Unit in Beirut. Here she counts and maps how often letters and their contextual forms repeat in running Arabic text, which behaves nothing like Latin. Part data, part visual experiment, 264 pages with a poster wrap. Pattern finding that changes how you design.

items.title: To design is also getting on a bus, gazing out the window and thinking on the move
items.note: Notes a Barcelona designer wrote on the H6 bus, which became a newsletter, then a book. Impostor syndrome, uncertainty, who gets to decide, and a case against constant digital urgency. Small, 160 pages, from Set Margins'. One to hand to anyone on your team who's running hot.

items.title: Logos of the Venezuelan Minitecas
items.note: Hundreds of logos from Venezuela's minitecas, the small sound systems that played electro, Miami bass and Italo disco from the 70s on. Compiled by Phran, part of Klasse Wrecks' pocket KFAX logo series. 70 pages, palm sized. Pure vernacular identity work, made by people who never called it that.

items.title: Partners #4
items.note: A Tokyo annual about relationships, one question per issue. This one asks "What do you follow?" and opens with butterflies and Tokuko Ushioda's photos of more than 100 fridges. Designed by Julie Peeters, 400 pages in a compact book format. A study in pacing, like her Bill.

items.title: Slanted Experimental Type 4.0
items.note: The fourth round from students at Dortmund, led by Lars Harmsen and Andreas Ruhe. Typefaces built from accidents, imprecision and odd systems, including variable and AI-made fonts. 296 pages. Not all of it will land, but it's a good look at where students are pushing type.

items.title: Jurriaan Schrofer (1926 to 1990)
items.note: Not new (2014), but on Counter-Print's shelf and worth knowing. Schrofer did photobooks, brochures, magazines and typefaces, and spent years on optical effects and perspective in type. 424 pages, designed by Jaap van Triest and Karel Martens, so it pairs well with the Martens books from earlier lists.

items.title: Amphorae: An Incomplete Compendium of Non-Ancient Greek Vessels
items.note: 157 drawings of made-up amphorae, some close to the real thing, some not at all, many carrying hand-lettered lines like "Can I Pet Your Dog?". A tiny 320-page softcover from Hyper Hypo in Athens. Light relief, and a smart riff on decoration as message.

items.title: Fons Hickmann m23
items.note: Hickmann co-founded the Berlin studio in 2001 with Gesine Grotrian-Steinweg. Conceptual posters, books and identity systems, and he has led the 100 Beste Plakate poster association since 2018. He teaches at the Berlin University of the Arts too. Follow for the posters.
